description: Expanded 94-line game-show host phrase pack with Chesterfield / Mansfield / Worksop banter and Trakway safety-topic callouts.

voiceSpec.accent: Chesterfield / Mansfield / Worksop; East Midlands with Yorkshire-border flavour
voiceSpec.mood: fun, energetic, quick-witted, dry site banter, confident game-show host, never cartoonishly exaggerated

scriptDescription: Game-show host phrases for all stages of Robbo’s Trakway Trivia: intros, question lead-ins, correct/wrong responses, score transitions, outros, plus contextual Trakway safety lines.

phrases.text: Ey up, youth — welcome to Robbo’s Trakway Trivia. Reet then, no hiding behind the brew this time.
Right, troops. Helmets on, brains switched on — Robbo’s Trakway Trivia is live.
Ey up. Chesterfield, Mansfield, Worksop — settle thi arguments. We’re finding out who actually knows the job.
Welcome in. It’s Trakway knowledge, site banter and absolutely no points for looking confident.
Robbo’s in the chair. Teams ready? Good. Let’s see who’s been listening and who’s just been waiting for brew.
Here’s thi next one — nice and steady.
Reet, youth, get thi sen round this one.
No shouting from the back. Here comes the question.
This one separates operators from professional brew drinkers.
Think before tha taps. There’s no rewind on site and none in Robbo’s quiz either.
Right then — what would tha actually do, not what sounds clever in the canteen?
Reet job, youth — panel’s in.
That’s the one. Proper answer, properly locked in.
Bang on. Somebody’s actually read the method statement.
Correct. Tha can keep thi imaginary hi-vis for another round.
Spot on. Robbo approves — and that’s rarer than an empty brew queue.
Correct answer. Clean lift, clean point.
Yes, youth. That’s exactly it.
Nailed it. No drama, no waffle, just the right answer.
Close, sen, but we don’t install panels on close.
Nope. Tha’s sent that one straight into the purple zone.
Wrong answer. Somewhere, a lift supervisor has just sighed.
Not this time, youth. Have another brew and think about thi choices.
That’s gone a bit Worksop on a Friday afternoon.
Robbo says no. Back to the method statement with thee.
Wrong one. Good news is nobody’s actually lifted owt.
That answer’s got more wobble than a panel in a crosswind.
Clamp question. Don’t guess — what matters before that panel leaves the deck?
If tha doesn’t know the clamp SWL, tha doesn’t know whether tha can make the lift. Simple as that.
Correct — capacity has to suit the load and the planned configuration. No pub maths.
Wrong — the clamp looking sturdy is not a lifting calculation, youth.
Wind limit next. Remember, gusts count as weather as well.
If the wind’s outside the limit, what’s Robbo’s favourite lifting technique? Stop.
Correct — conditions get checked against the lift plan, not against how brave everybody feels.
Wrong — ‘it’ll be reet’ is not a wind-speed control measure.
Zone question. Red means what, purple means what — and who should be where?
Don’t let the colours fool thee. The exclusion controls only work if people respect them.
Correct — keep people out of the danger area and control access properly.
If somebody wanders into the wrong zone, the lift pauses. No debate, no heroics.
Test lift. Small movement, big information — what are we proving before committing?
Correct — prove the load, attachment and control before carrying on with the full lift.
Wrong — a test lift is not the ceremonial bit we skip because everyone looks busy.
Nice one. Controlled test first, then proceed when everything behaves as planned.
Paddles next. They’re there to control the load, not decorate the truck.
Correct — use the planned handling aids and keep hands out of the danger areas.
Wrong — grabbing the panel because it’s quicker is exactly how quick jobs become incidents.
Reet. Good paddle control, good body position, much less shouting.
Sockets and connections — check them before tha commits the lift.
Correct. Positive connection, proper inspection, no wishful thinking.
Wrong. If the connection is damaged, doubtful or not seated, the answer is stop and sort it.
A socket isn’t ‘nearly in’. It’s either correctly engaged or it isn’t.
Communication question. One lift, one clear system, no committee meeting over the radio.
Correct — agreed signals, clear responsibility and no mixed instructions.
Wrong — three people shouting different things does not equal extra supervision.
If communication is lost, what happens? Correct: the movement stops until control is restored.
Exclusion zone now. Who actually needs to be inside it? As few people as the job genuinely requires.
Correct — establish it, maintain it and challenge anyone entering without a reason.
Wrong — cones by themselves don’t manage people. Supervision does.
The exclusion zone travels with the risk, youth. Don’t leave the danger and move the barrier.
Overhead lines. GS6 time — this is not the round for guesswork.
Correct — identify the hazard, set the controls and keep the safe clearance arrangements intact.
Wrong — goalposts are a control, not permission to forget where the conductors are.
If the set-up changes, recheck the overhead-line risk. Yesterday’s measurement is not today’s guarantee.
Good answer. Electricity does not care how experienced the crew is.
Team question. Everybody has a job, but that doesn’t mean everybody gives lifting instructions.
Correct — roles are defined before the lift so responsibility doesn’t become a group mystery.
Wrong — ‘we all know what we’re doing’ is how nobody knows who was meant to stop it.
One team, clear roles, clean communication. That’s the boring stuff that keeps the exciting stuff safe.
Ground conditions next. A stable crane starts with what’s underneath it.
Correct — check support, bearing conditions and the planned stabiliser arrangement before loading it.
Wrong — flat-looking ground and suitable ground are not the same thing.
If the set-up doesn’t match the plan, stop and reassess before lifting.
Dynamic risk assessment — not a tick-box, a live check of what’s actually changed.
Correct — if conditions differ from the plan, assess the change and control it before proceeding.
Wrong — the method statement does not magically update itself when the site changes.
Good. New hazard, new assessment, then a decision. Not the other way round.
Stop-work question. What happens when something doesn’t feel controlled? Tha stops.
Correct — anyone identifying an unsafe condition can call the stop. Sort it before restarting.
Wrong — schedule pressure is not a control measure.
Robbo likes this answer: stop, make safe, reassess, then continue only when the controls are back.
No points are worth forcing a lift. Same goes for real jobs.
Responsible Person round. Who owns the operational decision when the agreed controls can’t be maintained?
Correct — escalate to the person with the authority to resolve the issue, not the nearest bloke with a radio.
Wrong — responsibility doesn’t disappear because everybody is busy.
If the job has moved outside the planned conditions, the Responsible Person needs the right information before it carries on.
Scores are tightening up. Suddenly everybody remembers the training.
Halfway there. Chesterfield’s talking big, Mansfield’s counting points and Worksop’s asking for a recount already.
Next round coming up. Forget the last one — unless tha got it right, then mention it repeatedly.
It’s close at the top. One daft answer could change everything.
Final few questions. This is where confident people become very interested in the floor.
That’s thi lot. Scores locked, reputations slightly damaged, Trakway knowledge hopefully improved.
Game over. If tha won, act surprised. If tha lost, blame Robbo’s accent.
Reet, excellent work. Take the banter, keep the learning and use the controls properly when it actually matters.
Robbo’s Trakway Trivia is done. Brew time — and somebody check Mansfield hasn’t edited the scoreboard.
